sentences.nl: Vandaag oefenen we de grammatica van #dutchgrammar 2 les 18 over de woorden te, iets en die in combinatie met een bijvoeglijk naamwoord, maar zonder een zelfstandig naamwoord.
sentences.en: Today we practise the grammar of #dutchgrammar 2 lesson 18, about the words te, iets and die combined with an adjective, but without a noun.
sentences.note: Boilerplate.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Today practice we the grammar of #dutchgrammar 2 lesson 18 about the words to, something, and that in combination with an adjective, but without a noun.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses "Vandaag oefenen we," which follows the common Dutch word order of time-manner-place: time ("Vandaag"), verb ("oefenen"), and subject ("we").  
• The verbs "oefenen" (to practice) and "zijn" (to be) can be used with various objects or clauses.  
• The structure "iets en die in combinatie met" (something and that in combination with) is used to describe the combination of elements.  
• Example 1: "Vandaag leren we over de geschiedenis van Nederland." (Today we learn about the history of the Netherlands.)  
• Example 2: "We oefenen met het gebruik van voorzetsels in zinnen." (We practice with the use of prepositions in sentences.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Morgen bespreken we de regels van #dutchgrammar 3 les 5 over werkwoorden." (Tomorrow we will discuss the rules of #dutchgrammar 3 lesson 5 about verbs.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The use of hashtags like "#dutchgrammar" in educational contexts is common in social media to categorize content and make it easily searchable for learners.

sentences.nl: Martin heeft net gedag tegen Lars gezegd.
sentences.en: Martin has just said goodbye to Lars.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Martin has just goodbye to Lars said.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Heeft gezegd" is the present perfect tense, which is used to indicate a completed action.  
• "Net" means "just" and is used to indicate that the action happened recently.  
• "Gedag zeggen" is a fixed expression meaning "to say goodbye."  
• Example: "Ik heb net gegeten." (I have just eaten.)  
• Example: "Zij heeft net een boek gelezen." (She has just read a book.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Anna heeft net een cadeau aan Tom gegeven." (Anna has just given a gift to Tom.)

## 4. Culture Note  
• In the Netherlands, saying goodbye often involves a casual "doei" or "dag," and it's common to give a wave or a nod, depending on the level of formality.

gedag.form_note: used in the expression 'gedag zeggen' (to say goodbye)

collocations.head: iets tegen iemand zeggen (over iets)
collocations.en: to say sth to sb (about sth)

sentences.nl: Hij komt Gianluca tegen met iets moois.
sentences.en: He runs into Gianluca with something beautiful.
sentences.note: iets moois — rule B: iets + adjective + s.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• He comes Gianluca against with something beautiful.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Komt...tegen" is a separable verb "tegenkomen," which means "to meet" or "to encounter." The word "tegen" is placed at the end of the clause.  
• "Iets moois" uses "iets" (something) followed by an adjective in its noun form, "moois," meaning "something beautiful."  
• Examples:  
  - "Wij komen vaak oude vrienden tegen." (We often meet old friends.)  
  - "Ik kwam een leuke winkel tegen." (I came across a nice shop.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij komt haar leraar tegen met iets interessants. (She encounters her teacher with something interesting.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, it's common to encounter people unexpectedly in small towns or neighborhoods due to the compact nature of many communities.

gianluca.form_note: proper noun, name of a person

tegen.form_note: used here in the context of 'runs into'

moois.form_note: used as a noun with 'iets', meaning 'something beautiful'

grammarHits.explanation: iets + mooi with no noun after it → mooi + s: 'something beautiful' (the flowers).

sentences.nl: Een grote bos bloemen.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• A large bunch of flowers.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Een" is the indefinite article "a" or "an."  
• "Grote" is the adjective "large" or "big," and it agrees with the noun in gender and number, taking an -e ending here.  
• "Bos" means "bunch" or "bouquet."  
• "Bloemen" is the plural form of "bloem," meaning "flowers."

– Example 1: "Een kleine bos bloemen." (A small bunch of flowers.)  
– Example 2: "Een mooie bos bloemen." (A beautiful bunch of flowers.)  
– Example 3: "Een grote doos boeken." (A large box of books.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Een grote mand appels." (A large basket of apples.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, giving flowers is a common gesture for various occasions, including birthdays, anniversaries, and as a thank you gift. Flowers are often sold in markets and shops, and the Dutch are known for their love of floral arrangements.

grote.form_note: inflected form of groot to agree with the noun bos

sentences.nl: Hoi Gianluca, zegt Martin.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Hi Gianluca, says Martin.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses direct speech where "zegt" is the third person singular present tense of "zeggen" (to say).  
• Dutch often uses a comma before the name in direct speech to separate the greeting from the person being addressed.  
• Word order in Dutch is Subject-Verb-Object (SVO) in main clauses.

Extra Examples:  
• "Hallo Anna, roept Pieter." (Hello Anna, shouts Pieter.)  
• "Dag Marie, antwoordt Jan." (Good day Marie, answers Jan.)  
• "Hoi iedereen, zegt de leraar." (Hi everyone, says the teacher.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Hoi Lisa, vraagt Tom." (Hi Lisa, asks Tom.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Dutch greetings are typically informal, and "Hoi" is a very common way to say hello among friends and peers.

sentences.nl: Eh, hoi Martin.
Voor wie zijn die bloemen?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• For whom are those flowers?

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses an inversion structure where the preposition "voor" (for) and the interrogative pronoun "wie" (whom) come first, followed by the verb "zijn" (are) and the subject "die bloemen" (those flowers). This is typical for forming questions in Dutch.  
• "Voor wie" is a common phrase used to ask about the recipient or purpose of something.  
• Example phrases:  
  - Voor wie is deze taart? (For whom is this cake?)  
  - Voor wie werk jij? (For whom do you work?)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Voor wie is dat cadeau? (For whom is that gift?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Flowers play a significant role in Dutch culture, with the Netherlands being a major exporter of flowers, especially tulips. Offering flowers is a common gesture for various occasions.

zijn.form_note: conjugated form of 'zijn' for plural subjects

die.form_note: used with plural nouns or de-words

sentences.nl: Eh, welke?
Die rode natuurlijk.
sentences.note: Die rode: noun (bloemen) dropped, adjective keeps -e (rule C). rood → rode.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• That red one naturally.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Die" is a demonstrative pronoun meaning "that" for de-words or plural nouns.  
• "Rode" is the adjective "red," here used with a definite pronoun, hence the -e ending.  
• "Natuurlijk" means "naturally" or "of course," often used to emphasize an obvious choice or fact.

• Examples:  
  - "Die grote hond." (That big dog.)  
  - "Die blauwe natuurlijk." (That blue one naturally.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Die groene is mijn favoriet." (That green one is my favorite.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None

die.form_note: used for plural nouns or singular de-nouns

grammarHits.explanation: The noun bloemen is dropped because it's obvious; rood keeps its -e (and loses one o: rood → rode).

sentences.nl: Oh, die.
Eh, ja.
Eh, Martin, ik moet je iets bekennen.
sentences.en: Uh, Martin, I have to confess something to you.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Eh, Martin, I must you something confess.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses "moet" (must), which is a modal verb. Modal verbs typically require the main verb to be in the infinitive form, which is why "bekennen" (to confess) is at the end of the sentence.  
• The structure "ik moet je iets bekennen" (I must confess something to you) places the direct object "iets" (something) before the infinitive verb, which is common in Dutch.  
• Example 1: Ik moet je iets vertellen. (I must tell you something.)  
• Example 2: Ik moet je iets geven. (I must give you something.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Eh, Lisa, ik moet je iets zeggen. (Eh, Lisa, I must tell you something.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The use of "Eh" in Dutch is a casual way to get someone's attention, similar to "um" or "uh" in English, often used when someone is hesitant or unsure. It's informal and common in everyday conversation.

sentences.nl: Misschien iets onverwachts voor jou.
sentences.note: iets onverwachts — rule B.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Maybe something unexpected for you.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Misschien" is an adverb meaning "maybe" or "perhaps," placed at the beginning of the sentence to indicate uncertainty or possibility.  
• "Iets" means "something" and is used here as an indefinite pronoun.  
• "Onverwachts" is an adjective meaning "unexpected." In Dutch, adjectives can be used without a noun when the noun is implied, as in this case.  
• "Voor" is a preposition meaning "for," used here to indicate the recipient of the unexpected thing.  
• Example 1: "Misschien is het morgen beter." (Maybe it will be better tomorrow.)  
• Example 2: "Hij heeft iets belangrijks te vertellen." (He has something important to tell.)  
• Example 3: "Dit is voor jou." (This is for you.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Misschien komt er iets moois op je pad. (Maybe something beautiful will come your way.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None.

iets.form_note: used with adjectives in -s to mean 'something [adjective]'

grammarHits.explanation: iets + onverwacht, no noun → onverwacht + s: 'something unexpected'.

sentences.nl: Ja, ik vind Marieke ook leuk.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Yes, I find Marieke also nice.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ja" means "yes" and is used for affirmation.  
• "Ik vind" translates to "I find," where "vind" is the present-tense form of "vinden" (to find). This structure is used to express opinions or feelings about someone or something.  
• "ook" means "also," indicating agreement or similarity in opinion.  
• "leuk" means "nice" or "fun," commonly used for expressing positive opinions about people or activities.

Extra Sentences:  
• "Ik vind de film leuk." (I find the movie nice.)  
• "Hij vindt het boek ook interessant." (He finds the book also interesting.)  
• "Wij vinden haar aardig." (We find her kind.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Ja, ik vind die hond ook schattig." (Yes, I find that dog also cute.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, being direct about your opinions, such as saying you find someone "leuk," is common and not considered rude. It's a straightforward way to express liking or approval.

vind.form_note: conjugated form, first person singular present tense

sentences.nl: Deze bloemen zijn voor haar.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• These flowers are for her.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Deze" is a demonstrative pronoun meaning "these," used for plural nouns.  
• The sentence structure follows a simple Subject-Verb-Object order: "Deze bloemen" (subject) + "zijn" (verb) + "voor haar" (object with preposition).  
• "Voor" is a preposition meaning "for" and is used to indicate the recipient.  
• Example 1: "Dit cadeau is voor jou." (This gift is for you.)  
• Example 2: "Deze boeken zijn voor de bibliotheek." (These books are for the library.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Die kaarten zijn voor ons." (Those tickets are for us.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, giving flowers is a common gesture for various occasions, such as birthdays, celebrations, or as a thank you. Different flowers can symbolize different sentiments.

deze.form_note: used for plural nouns and singular de-nouns

sentences.nl: Ik weet dat jij een goede vriend bent, maar ik vind Marieke gewoon te leuk om te laten lopen.
sentences.en: I know you are a good friend, but I simply like Marieke too much to let her go.
sentences.note: te leuk om te laten lopen: first te = too (rule A), second te = infinitive. And 🔴 the om … te frame.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• I know that you a good friend are, but I find Marieke just too nice to let walk.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses a subordinate clause structure with "dat" (that), which sends the verb to the end of the clause: "jij een goede vriend bent" (you are a good friend).  
• "Te leuk om te laten lopen" (too nice to let walk) uses the construction "te + adjective + om te + verb" to express "too [adjective] to [verb]."  
• "Gewoon" (just) can be used for emphasis or to indicate something is straightforward.  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Ik denk dat zij het boek leest." (I think that she is reading the book.)  
  - "Het is te warm om buiten te spelen." (It is too hot to play outside.)  
  - "Hij is gewoon de baas." (He is just the boss.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ze zegt dat hij een slimme leerling is, maar hij is gewoon te verlegen om op te vallen. (She says that he is a smart student, but he is just too shy to stand out.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, directness is valued, so expressing feelings like 'vind Marieke gewoon te leuk' (find Marieke just too nice) is typically accepted and appreciated for its honesty.

goede.form_note: inflected form of 'goed' for common gender singular nouns

marieke.form_note: proper noun, name of a person

om.form_note: used with te + infinitive to indicate purpose

grammarHits.explanation: te before an adjective = too: 'too nice (to let go)'. The te in om te laten is the other te — infinitive, not 'too'.

collocations.head: om … te
collocations.en: (in order) to … — the Dutch infinitive clause

sentences.nl: Oh, maar wat bedoel je?
sentences.en: Oh, but what do you mean?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Oh, but what do you mean?

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Oh" is an interjection used to express surprise or realization.  
• "maar" means "but," and is used here to indicate a contrast or hesitation.  
• "wat" translates to "what," functioning as a question word.  
• "bedoel" is the first-person singular present tense of "bedoelen," meaning "to mean."  
• "je" is the informal singular form of "you."

Extra Dutch phrases:
- "Maar waarom vraag je dat?" (But why do you ask that?)
- "Wat zeg je?" (What are you saying?)
- "Ik bedoel dat het belangrijk is." (I mean that it is important.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Oh, maar hoe weet je dat?" (Oh, but how do you know that?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None

sentences.nl: Jij vindt Marieke toch ook een leuk meisje?
sentences.en: You think Marieke is a nice girl too, don't you?
sentences.note: een leuk meisje: een + het-word → no -e (les 5, rule B).
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• You find Marieke still also a nice girl?

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Jij vindt" is the present tense form of "vinden" (to find) for "jij" (you).  
• "Toch" is used for emphasis, often to confirm something you assume to be true, similar to "still" or "right" in English.  
• The sentence order is subject (jij) - verb (vindt) - direct object (Marieke) - adverb (toch ook) - complement (een leuk meisje).  
• Example: "Jij hebt toch ook die film gezien?" (You have seen that movie too, right?)  
• Example: "Hij is toch ook een goede vriend?" (He is a good friend too, right?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Zij denkt toch ook dat het een goed idee is?" (She thinks it’s a good idea too, right?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, using "toch" can soften the tone of a question, making it less direct or confrontational, which aligns with the Dutch preference for politeness and consensus in conversation.

sentences.nl: Ik eh…
Martin denkt dat Marieke en Gianluca verliefd op elkaar zijn.
sentences.en: Martin thinks that Marieke and Gianluca are in love with each other.
sentences.note: dat-clause: verb zijn goes to the end (BS-05).
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Martin thinks that Marieke and Gianluca in love with each other are.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses indirect speech with "denkt dat" (thinks that), which introduces a subordinate clause.  
• "Verliefd op elkaar zijn" (in love with each other are) is a phrase where "verliefd" (in love) requires the preposition "op" (on) to indicate who is the object of affection.  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Zij denkt dat hij een goede kok is." (She thinks that he is a good cook.)  
  - "Wij zijn verliefd op dezelfde film." (We are in love with the same movie.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Lisa gelooft dat Tom en Anna boos op elkaar zijn. (Lisa believes that Tom and Anna are angry with each other.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, open discussions about relationships and feelings can be quite common, reflecting a direct communication style.

sentences.nl: En hij wil niet toegeven dat hij Marieke eerst ook wilde.
sentences.en: And he doesn't want to admit that at first he wanted Marieke too.
sentences.note: dat hij Marieke eerst ook wilde: verb last (BS-05), and eerst ook sit before it in the middle (BS-07).
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• And he wants not admit that he Marieke first also wanted.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "En hij wil niet toegeven" uses the modal verb "wil" (wants) followed by the infinitive "toeggeven" (to admit), which is a common structure in Dutch for expressing desires or intentions.  
• "dat hij Marieke eerst ook wilde" uses a subordinate clause introduced by "dat" (that), which pushes the verb "wilde" (wanted) to the end of the clause, a typical feature in Dutch grammar.

• Example: "Zij kan niet geloven dat hij haar vergeten is." (She cannot believe that he has forgotten her.)  
• Example: "Hij zegt dat hij morgen niet kan komen." (He says that he cannot come tomorrow.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hij wil niet toegeven dat hij het boek nog niet gelezen heeft. (He doesn't want to admit that he hasn't read the book yet.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• No cultural note.

sentences.nl: Dat vindt hij te moeilijk.
sentences.note: te moeilijk (rule A). Also inversion: Dat vindt hij.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• That finds he too difficult.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses a common Dutch structure with "vinden" (to find) where the opinion or perception is expressed. "Dat" (that) is the object, "vindt" is the conjugated verb, "hij" (he) is the subject, and "te moeilijk" (too difficult) is the predicate adjective.  
• The word order places the verb second, which is typical in Dutch main clauses.  
• The phrase "te moeilijk" is an example of using "te" (too) as an intensifier.  

Extra sentences:  
- "Dat vind ik leuk." (I find that nice.)  
- "Dit boek vindt zij interessant." (She finds this book interesting.)  
- "Hij vindt de film saai." (He finds the movie boring.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Dat vinden ze erg belangrijk." (They find that very important.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• No related culture notes.

moeilijk.form_note: base form, used with 'te' to indicate 'too difficult'

sentences.nl: Dus zegt hij: "Nee hoor, ik heb al een vriendin."
sentences.en: So he says: "No, I already have a girlfriend."
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• So says he: "No indeed, I have already a girlfriend."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dus zegt hij" follows Dutch inversion where the verb comes before the subject due to "dus" (so).  
• "Nee hoor" is an informal way to emphasize a negative response, similar to "No indeed" or "No, really."  
• "Ik heb al een vriendin" uses "al" to indicate "already," showing that something is presently true.  
  
Examples:  
- "Daarna gaat hij naar huis." (Afterwards, he goes home.)  
- "Ja hoor, ik ben klaar." (Yes indeed, I am ready.)  
- "Ik heb al gegeten." (I have already eaten.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Toen zei ze: "Ja hoor, ik ben al onderweg." (Then she said: "Yes indeed, I am already on my way.")

sentences.nl: Gianluca is verbaasd.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Gianluca is surprised.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence follows a simple subject-verb-complement structure, which is typical in Dutch. The verb "is" is the third-person singular form of "zijn" (to be).  
• The adjective "verbaasd" (surprised) is used to describe Gianluca's state.  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Zij is blij." (She is happy.)  
  - "Wij zijn moe." (We are tired.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Maria is nieuwsgierig." (Maria is curious.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• [No cultural note applicable.]

source.title: Grammar 2 les 18 — te, iets and die with an adjective (without a noun)

rules.name: te + adjective = too
rules.how: te right before an adjective or adverb means 'too'. Don't confuse it with te before an infinitive (te lezen, om … te vertellen), which just marks the verb.
examples: Hij heeft een te hoge fiets.

rules.name: iets / wat / niets … + adjective + s
rules.how: After a quantity word — iets, wat, niets, veel, weinig, genoeg, allerlei, meer, minder, voldoende — an adjective with no noun after it gets -s. English says 'something nice'; Dutch says iets leuks.

rules.name: die + adjective-e, noun left out
rules.how: When the noun is already clear, Dutch can drop it and keep the adjective with its -e: Welke appel? Die grote. Bart's advice on the slide: when you speak, just add the noun.
